title: Japan Has Been Here Before: The 1987 Persian Gulf Crisis
gist: With the Strait of Hormuz effectively closed since the U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran in February 2026, oil-import-dependent Japan faces surging gasoline prices and renewed pressure to contribute militarily to Gulf shipping security. Tsuruta Jun recalls the 1987 Iran-Iraq War tanker crisis, when Japan debated sending MSDF minesweepers and Coast Guard vessels but ultimately declined while European allies joined the U.S.-led effort.

themes.theme: Hormuz closure and Japan's energy exposure

insights.claim: The Strait of Hormuz has been effectively closed since the U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran in February 2026, leaving oil tankers unable to transit one of the world's most critical trade arteries.
insights.speaker: TSURUTA Jun
insights.so_what: A sustained Hormuz closure is a major oil supply shock, supporting elevated crude prices and tanker/insurance disruption globally.
insights.quote: The Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed following the U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran in February, leaving oil tankers unable to transit the strait
insights.locator: The Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed

insights.claim: Japan imports more than 90 percent of its crude oil from the Middle East, and gasoline prices in Japan have surged with wide-ranging effects on daily life.
insights.speaker: TSURUTA Jun
insights.so_what: Japan is among the most exposed major economies to a Hormuz shock, implying pressure on its trade balance, the yen and consumer inflation.
insights.quote: Japan imports more than 90 percent of its crude oil from the Middle East. Gasoline prices have surged
insights.locator: The Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed

insights.claim: During the Iran-Iraq War, the Japanese government actively debated sending Maritime Self-Defense Force minesweepers and Japan Coast Guard patrol vessels to the Persian Gulf, and ultimately chose not to.
insights.speaker: TSURUTA Jun
insights.so_what: Historical restraint frames the current debate over whether Japan will deploy forces to secure Gulf shipping — a test of its evolving security posture.
insights.quote: the Japanese government actively debated whether to send Maritime Self-Defense Force (MSDF) minesweepers and Japan Coast Guard (JCG) patrol vessels to the Persian Gulf — and ultimately chose not to
insights.locator: The current crisis has a precedent.

insights.claim: The Iran-Iraq War began with Iraq's invasion of Iran in September 1980 and spread to the sea around 1984, making Persian Gulf passage hazardous for tankers due to missile attacks and mines.
insights.speaker: TSURUTA Jun
insights.so_what: Shows Gulf shipping disruptions can persist for years once conflict moves to the sea.

insights.claim: In July 1987, at Kuwait's request, the U.S. began escorting tankers with warships, but a tanker still struck a mine, prompting Washington to ask Western countries including Japan to send minesweepers.
insights.speaker: TSURUTA Jun
insights.so_what: Naval escorts alone did not neutralize mine risk; demining capacity and allied burden-sharing are key to reopening chokepoints.
insights.quote: but a tanker still struck a mine

insights.claim: The U.K., France, Italy, the Netherlands and Belgium all contributed to the 1987 Gulf minesweeping effort, while Japan did not.
insights.speaker: TSURUTA Jun
insights.so_what: Japan's past non-participation contrasts with European burden-sharing, a precedent that may shape U.S. expectations of Tokyo in the current crisis.
insights.locator: The U.K., France, Italy, the Netherlands
